title: AI Email Workflow: Tame Your Inbox in 10-Minute Blocks

scenes.badge: Emails the average worker receives every day

chips.text: ≈ 1 hour a day at 30 s each

scenes.text: The average office worker now receives one hundred seventeen emails a day. That's according to Microsoft's twenty twenty five Work Trend Index, and it doesn't even count the one hundred fifty three chat messages on top. If each email took just thirty seconds, that would be almost an hour a day, just reading. In this video, I'll show you a simple workflow that uses free AI tools to get your inbox under control in short, ten minute sessions. I'll cover the method, the exact prompts, what's free and what costs money, and where AI gets email wrong.

scenes.chapterTitle: The one rule: AI drafts, you decide
scenes.title: AI drafts, you decide
scenes.sub: Speed up the boring parts. Keep the judgment.
scenes.text: Before we start, one rule runs through this whole video. AI drafts, you decide. AI is great at the boring parts of email: reading long threads, sorting, and writing a first draft. But it doesn't know your relationships, your promises, or what your boss really meant. So in this workflow, AI never sends anything on its own. It saves you the typing and the reading, and you keep the judgment. Also, I'm not promising a magic number of hours saved. I researched the tools and the method, and your results will depend on your inbox.

footer.text: The problem is the constant checking

scenes.text: Here's why email feels endless. Microsoft looked at how people use its work apps and called it the infinite workday. The average worker gets one hundred seventeen emails and one hundred fifty three Teams messages daily. People are interrupted by a meeting, email or notification about every two minutes. Forty percent of people online at six in the morning are already reviewing email. And by ten at night, twenty nine percent of active workers are checking their inbox again. The problem isn't one email. It's the constant checking.

items.text: Batch: check email at set times
Draft replies with AI, then edit

scenes.text: Here's the whole method in five steps. One, batch: open email two or three times a day at set times, instead of all day. Two, sort everything with four quick decisions. Three, summarize long threads with AI, so you don't read every message. Four, draft replies with AI, then edit them in your own voice. And five, automate the repeats with filters, so the same kinds of email stop landing in front of you. Each session should take about ten minutes. Let's go through them one by one.

scenes.chapterTitle: Sort every email with the 4 Ds

items.name: Delete
items.desc: Won't need it? Archive it right away

items.name: Delegate
items.desc: Someone else's job? Forward with one line

items.name: Defer
items.desc: Real work? Make it a dated task, then archive

scenes.text: Step one is simple: close the inbox between sessions. Step two is where the time goes, so use the four Ds. Delete: if you won't need it, archive it right away. Do: if a reply takes under two minutes, answer it now. Delegate: if someone else should handle it, forward it with one clear line. Defer: if it needs real work, turn it into a task with a date, and archive the email. Every message gets one of those four decisions, once. You stop rereading the same email five times.

scenes.chapterTitle: Gemini in Gmail: free vs paid
scenes.text: Good news: in Gmail, the core AI tools are now free. In January twenty twenty six, Google made thread summaries, Help me write and suggested replies free for personal accounts, starting in the US in English. That's zero dollars for steps three and four. The paid features come with Google AI Plus, at four ninety nine a month, which adds the Gemini side panel, Proofread and the AI Inbox. Google AI Pro, at nineteen ninety nine, adds smarter search across your email. Outside the US, any chatbot can do the same steps. Prices checked November twenty twenty six.

items.text: Ask for decisions, questions, my to-dos
Check it against the latest message

scenes.text: Step three: summarize. Start with your longest threads, because that's where reading time hides. In Gmail, tap the summary at the top of the conversation. In any other chatbot, ask this: summarize this thread in three bullets, list any decisions made, any open questions, and anything I'm expected to do, with dates. Then check the summary against the latest message, because summaries can miss a late change of plan. Verify before you act. A forty message thread becomes a thirty second read, and you only open the original when something looks important.

scenes.chapterTitle: Draft replies with one prompt formula

items.text: Who it's for, and the goal
The key facts, in your words

footer.text: Never send an AI draft unread

scenes.text: Step four: draft replies. A vague request gets a vague email, so give the AI three things. Who the reply is for, and the goal. The key facts, written in your own words, like dates, prices or a yes or no. And the tone and length, for example friendly, under eighty words. In Gmail, that's Help me write. Then edit it: cut the fluff, fix any detail the AI guessed, and make it sound like you. One rule here. Never send an AI draft unread. Your name is on it, not the tool's.

items.name: Unsubscribe
items.desc: Newsletters you never open? Leave them

items.name: Filters
items.desc: Receipts and alerts skip the inbox

items.name: Templates
items.desc: Save replies you send every week

footer.text: Every rule removes a type of email for good

scenes.text: Step five: automate the repeats. This step costs nothing and keeps paying off. First, unsubscribe from newsletters you never open. Second, create filters, so receipts, shipping updates and app alerts skip the inbox and go straight to a folder. Third, use labels for the senders that matter, like bills, your team or clients. And fourth, save templates for replies you send every week. If you don't know how to set up a filter, ask a chatbot to explain the steps for your email app. Every rule you set removes a type of email forever.

chips.text: Upgrade only if you outgrow it

scenes.text: Do you need a paid email app? For most people, probably not. Here's the ladder, checked November twenty twenty six. Gmail's built-in AI is free in the US. Google AI Plus is four ninety nine a month. Dedicated apps cost more. Shortwave has a free plan with basic AI summaries, but it adds a sent with Shortwave signature to your emails. Superhuman, a premium email app, costs about twenty five to thirty dollars per user a month. Those apps are built for people who live in email all day. Start free, and upgrade only if you outgrow it.

items.name: Invented
items.desc: Dates, prices or promises that aren't real

items.name: Wrong tone
items.desc: Too stiff, too cheerful or too long

items.name: No context
items.desc: Doesn't know your history with people

items.name: Privacy
items.desc: Never paste passwords or client secrets

scenes.text: Now the honest part. Here's where AI gets email wrong. It can invent details, like a date, a price or a promise you never made. It can get the tone wrong, too stiff for a friend or too cheerful for bad news. It misses context, like your history with that person. Privacy matters too: don't paste passwords, client secrets or other people's personal data into a chatbot, and check your company's AI policy for work email. And be careful with anything that sends automatically, because you can't unsend a mistake. AI drafts, you decide.

items.text: 1 min: one new filter or unsubscribe

scenes.text: Here's how it fits into ten minutes. First two minutes: read the AI summaries of your longest threads. Next three minutes: sort everything else with the four Ds. Next four minutes: draft and edit your replies with AI. Last minute: add one new filter, or unsubscribe from one sender. Do this two or three times a day, at set times, and close the inbox in between. The filters add up, so the inbox gets lighter over time. Try it for two weeks and notice how often you still open email between sessions.

scenes.title: Own your inbox
scenes.next: Dollar-Cost Averaging: The Boring Strategy That Works
scenes.text: Email won't disappear, but it doesn't have to run your day. Batch it, sort it with the four Ds, let AI summarize and draft, and automate the repeats. Which part of your inbox wastes the most time right now? Tell me in the comments. I read them. If this helped, subscribe to Future Money Lab, and share it with a coworker who's drowning in email. Next up, dollar cost averaging, the boring investing strategy that works.
